Cybersecurity Analyst Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A cybersecurity analyst resume has one job: prove you reduce risk, not just that you watch screens. Hiring managers do not hire for tool lists, alert counts, or certificates alone. They hire for incidents contained before they spread, vulnerabilities closed before attackers found them, and reports clear enough that managers acted on them: the threat you faced, the action you took, the risk it removed, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: A cybersecurity analyst resume should include a summary naming your security domain and strongest defence result, a skills section with SIEM, incident response, vulnerability management, and threat analysis, experience bullets pairing each incident or vulnerability with the risk it removed, and metrics showing faster detection, fewer successful attacks, and cleaner audits. Contained incidents beat tool lists alone.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: threat + action + risk removed — the alert you triaged, the incident you contained, the vulnerability you closed.
  • Lead with your domain and your headline defence result: SOC monitoring, incident response, or vulnerability management, with detection faster, attacks fewer, or audits cleaner.
  • Spell tools and frameworks exactly as postings do — SIEM, Splunk, Sentinel, CrowdStrike, NIST, MITRE ATT&CK — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show judgment under pressure, not just volume: the false positive you tuned out, the escalation you got right, and the incident you contained at 2am all prove analyst thinking.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a security lead what separates a keep-forever analyst from a risky one and it won’t be “passionate about security.” It’ll be:

  • Triage judgment. Alerts sorted fast and honestly — real threats escalated, false positives tuned out, and nothing important left sitting in the queue.
  • Containment under pressure. Hosts isolated, accounts disabled, and phishing campaigns blocked while the incident was still small, not after it spread.
  • Vulnerabilities closed, not just found. Scans run, findings prioritised by real risk, remediation tracked until closed, and re-scans proving it.
  • Reports managers act on. Incident write-ups with timeline, impact, and next steps, written so a non-technical manager can decide in minutes.
  • Learning from every incident. Detection rules improved, playbooks updated, and the same incident made harder to repeat — tracked after the alert, not assumed.

Cybersecurity Analyst Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for a cybersecurity analyst in a security operations centre. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: threat, action, risk removed.

AMARA NWOSU
Lagos · (234) 555-0147 · amara.nwosu@email.com · linkedin.com/in/amaranwosu

SUMMARY
Cybersecurity analyst with 4 years in SOC monitoring and incident response. Triaged 90 alerts a week, contained 34 confirmed incidents, cut critical vulnerabilities 62%, and closed every audit finding on time. Known for calm triage and reports managers act on.

SKILLS
SIEM · Splunk · Microsoft Sentinel · Incident response · Threat analysis · Vulnerability management · Phishing investigation · Endpoint detection (CrowdStrike) · MITRE ATT&CK · NIST controls · Network basics · Incident reporting

CERTIFICATIONS
CompTIA Security+ — 2022 · CompTIA CySA+ — 2024

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Cybersecurity Analyst — Shieldbank Financial, Lagos | 2022–Present

  • Own alert triage and incident response for a 1,200-endpoint banking environment: SIEM queues, endpoint alerts, phishing reports, and vulnerability remediation.
  • Triaged 90 alerts a week in Splunk and Sentinel, cutting mean time to detect from 47 minutes to 11 minutes by tuning 23 noisy rules and writing 9 new detections.
  • Contained 34 confirmed incidents, including a phishing campaign that reached 60 mailboxes: isolated 14 hosts, disabled 6 compromised accounts, and blocked the sender domain within 2 hours of the first report.
  • Ran the vulnerability programme across 1,200 endpoints, cutting critical vulnerabilities 62% in a year by prioritising internet-facing flaws and tracking remediation to re-scan.
  • Wrote 40 incident reports with timeline, impact, and next steps, and closed every audit finding on time across 2 annual audits with zero repeat findings.

IT Support Specialist — Northgate Logistics, Lagos | 2020–2022

  • Supported 300 users across 4 offices, handling account lockouts, phishing reports, and patching — the work that led into a security role.
  • Investigated 120 phishing reports, escalating 18 genuine attempts and cutting repeat clicks by training the 3 teams hit most often.
  • Tracked patching for 300 workstations, lifting on-time patching from 71% to 96% in 6 months by chasing owners weekly instead of monthly.
  • Documented account-access reviews for 2 audits, flagging 27 dormant accounts that were then disabled.

EDUCATION
BSc, Computer Science — 2020

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: domain, tenure, and headline proof in three lines

The example opens with domain and tenure, then the proof: alerts triaged, incidents contained, vulnerabilities cut, audits closed clean. Without a SOC title yet, lead with security scope: “built a home lab with a SIEM, triaged simulated alerts, and documented findings with remediation steps.”

Skills: tools and frameworks exactly as postings spell them

Security postings are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Name your tools (SIEM, Splunk, Sentinel, CrowdStrike) and your frameworks (NIST, MITRE ATT&CK). “Security-minded” is not a keyword; “incident response” is.

Experience: every bullet pairs a threat with the risk removed

The pattern is threat + action + result: “contained a phishing campaign by isolating hosts and disabling accounts within 2 hours”; “cut critical vulnerabilities by prioritising internet-facing flaws.” Scope matters too — endpoints covered, alerts per week, incidents contained.

Judgment: show the escalation you got right

Every analyst triages alerts; the strong ones also show judgment: the noisy rule tuned out, the genuine attempt escalated fast, the repeat finding closed for good. One bullet about a false positive fixed at the source proves the analyst thinking hiring managers pay for, and separates a cybersecurity analyst resume from a tool list.

Cybersecurity Analyst Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Monitoring: SIEM, Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, alert triage, log analysis, endpoint detection, network monitoring.
  • Response: incident response, containment, eradication, phishing investigation, malware triage, incident reporting.
  • Vulnerability: vulnerability scanning, remediation tracking, patch management, risk prioritisation, re-scanning (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK, NIST controls, security awareness training, access reviews, audit support.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Cybersecurity analyst resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost Cybersecurity Analyst Interviews

  1. Tool lists instead of incidents. “Used Splunk and CrowdStrike” says nothing about what you stopped. Every bullet needs a threat, an action, and a risk removed.
  2. Alert volume without outcomes. Alerts triaged is activity, not impact. Pair volume with detection time cut, incidents contained, or vulnerabilities closed — or leave the bullet out.
  3. Certifications without hands-on bullets. A certificate proves study, not judgment. Pair each one with work that used it: the detection you wrote, the incident you contained.
  4. Vague security language. “Ensured security” and “handled threats” mean nothing to a hiring manager. Name the threat, the tool, and the result: phishing campaign, hosts isolated, accounts disabled.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your incident-response section arrives as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a cybersecurity analyst resume?

A summary naming your security domain (e.g. cybersecurity analyst with 4 years in SOC monitoring and incident response) and strongest defence result; a skills section with SIEM, incident response, vulnerability management, and threat analysis; experience bullets pairing each incident or vulnerability with the risk it removed; and metrics showing faster detection, fewer successful attacks, and cleaner audits. Contained incidents beat tool lists alone.

Do I need a degree to become a cybersecurity analyst?

Not always — cybersecurity analysts come from computer science, information technology, networking, and military backgrounds, and many enter through IT support, helpdesk, or network operations roles plus certifications and home-lab work. Hiring managers weigh hands-on detection and response work far more than a specific degree. A degree helps for some employers, but a record of alerts triaged, incidents contained, and vulnerabilities closed proves more.

How do I make a cybersecurity analyst resume ATS-friendly?

Keep it single-column with standard headings (Summary, Skills, Experience, Education, Certifications) and real text, not an image of text. Spell tools and frameworks exactly as postings do (SIEM, Splunk, Sentinel, CrowdStrike, NIST, MITRE ATT&CK, vulnerability scanning), and save as a text-based PDF or DOCX. Run it through a free ATS grader before you apply — cybersecurity analyst resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting flair.

What skills do employers want most on a cybersecurity analyst resume?

Security monitoring and alert triage, incident response and containment, vulnerability management and remediation tracking, threat analysis and phishing investigation, identity and access basics, and clear incident reporting that non-technical managers can act on. Tool keywords matter: SIEM, Splunk, Sentinel, CrowdStrike, vulnerability scanning, and endpoint detection are literal ATS filters — spell them exactly as postings do, and name the risk behind each tool.

How do I write a cybersecurity analyst resume with no SOC experience yet?

Lead with security work you can show: a home lab where you monitored logs, triaged simulated alerts, and wrote up findings; a certification plus hands-on projects; or IT support work reframed as security work (account lockouts investigated, phishing reports handled, patching tracked). “Built a home lab with a SIEM, triaged 200 simulated alerts, and documented 12 findings with remediation steps” proves analyst thinking without a SOC title. Add relevant coursework and run it through a free ATS grader first.

Should a cybersecurity analyst resume list certifications?

Yes, when you hold them — certifications are one of the few signals applicant tracking systems and hiring managers both screen for in security roles. List them in their own section with the full name and year, and only list certifications you actually hold: CompTIA Security+, CySA+, ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity, and vendor training are common examples. A certification without matching hands-on bullets reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it.
